doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: Goodman, Hackett and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
title: World's Greatest Jazz Band and the Lawson-Haggart revival
summary: Joined through Hackett and Bob Haggart; six-horn front line, loose arrangements under Yank Lawson, the band's decline and the Legendary Lawson-Haggart Jazz Band recordings.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: That’s cool. How did The World’s Greatest Jazz Band come about?

Through Bobby Hackett. Vic Dickinson had been with the band and he took a leave and Benny Morton was filling in for Vic for a while, but I guess they didn’t know whether Benny was going to be a permanent member or not, and Bobby Hackett did say some nice things on my behalf, and Bob Haggart called me one time to do a date with them, and after that I joined the band and that was a marvelous experience.
There was quite a — gee you had, what four, five horns, I mean wind instruments?
Yeah there were two trumpets, two trombones, two reed instruments, that’s six in the front line.
So was the music arranged at all?

A lot of it was arranged, but a lot of it we didn’t use. I mean they arranged it for recording purposes, and sometimes I guess if it was expected, they would put up some arrangements on a concert and we would play them. But for the most part, Yank didn’t like to do that. I mean it was done, it was recorded and it was done, and he just felt there was much more freedom and flexibility in picking a tune and having everybody — you know it was such a nice experience because in ensemble playing, everybody had a certain place where they fit you know. And Yank knew how to make a statement as the lead trumpet player and leave space, and it seems like everyone else knew how not to over fill that space. It was as much fun, really, as playing the solos.
Wow. What about, was it tough financially to keep that kind of size group together at these times? This was what, the mid-70s?

‘75 I guess when I joined them. ‘75 or ‘76. And it was waning then. It was pretty good, I mean they did pretty well for a couple of years and then it just got a little bit more sparse. And I don’t think they cared. Because Yank was getting up in years and they had, you know, they were both great musicians and I think so much of a nice thing is fine, and then you want to go off in different directions. And they cut down the band eventually to just

the three horns, sometimes the four horn front line. And no reading, just picking tunes. In fact, later on we did some recording under the name of the Legendary Lawson-Haggart Jazz Band. Remember the old Lawson-Haggart records on Decca?
Well they revived that name and they called it the Legendary Lawson-Haggart Jazz Band. And we did some recording for Jazzology and Audiophile.
